result.summary: Pausanias traces the ancestry of Pyrrhus of Epirus back to Pyrrhus son of Achilles, and narrates the troubled succession in Epirus through Olympias, Æacides and Alcetas. He notes how Pyrrhus came to power and that he was the first Greek to war against the Romans.

scenes.title: Lineage of Pyrrhus of Epirus
scenes.summary: Pausanias explains how Pyrrhus is related to Alexander of Epirus and traces descent from Achilles' son Pyrrhus, who settled in Epirus. His sons and Helenus' son founded new settlements.

scenes.title: Troubles of Epirote Kings
scenes.summary: After Alexander's death, Olympias and Æacides fight Cassander's side and Æacides dies. Alcetas rules madly and is killed, and Pyrrhus is recalled.
scenes.stakes: Æacides and Alcetas risk their thrones and lives amid civil quarrels and Cassander's hostility.

scenes.title: Pyrrhus Regains Power, Fights Rome
scenes.summary: Pyrrhus flees to Ptolemy in Egypt, is restored, and takes Corcyra. Pausanias notes he was the first Greek to fight the Romans.
scenes.stakes: Pyrrhus risks losing his newly won kingdom to Cassander.

notable_quotes.reason: Marks Pyrrhus as the first Greek to make war on Rome.

analysis.text: Pausanias links a historical king to heroic Trojan-war ancestry, showing how Greek dynasties claimed mythical descent.
The passage records Hellenistic succession struggles after Alexander the Great, involving Macedonian, Epirote and Egyptian rulers.

legacy.text: Pyrrhus' costly wars against Rome gave the phrase 'Pyrrhic victory'.

fun_facts.text: Pausanias refers back to his earlier account of Lysimachus for Pyrrhus' Macedonian campaigns, showing his cross-referencing method.

language_notes.text: The syntax is garbled: Pyrrhus 'neglected' his home, i.e. gave up Thessaly and settled in Epirus, as Helenus' oracles directed.
'Equal share for each' means the sons replaced single kingship with a shared division of power among them.
'Met with her deserts' means she got the punishment she deserved.
'Uterine sister' means a half-sister sharing the same mother; here, Ptolemy's stepdaughter-like relation, a half-sister of his children.
'Already narrated' refers to Pausanias' earlier account of Lysimachus, in Chapter 9 of this book.
The 'disaster at Syracuse' is the destruction of Athens' Sicilian expedition (415–413 BC) during the Peloponnesian War.

context_notes.text: Pyrrhus is Neoptolemus, son of Achilles, called Pyrrhus here. Helenus was a Trojan seer who later settled in Epirus.
Pergamus is the city Pergamum in Asia Minor, later the capital of a famous kingdom.
Olympias was Alexander the Great's mother; she fought Cassander and the Macedonian rulers over the succession.
Ptolemy son of Lagus ruled Egypt after Alexander the Great, founding the Ptolemaic dynasty.
Pyrrhus invaded Italy in 280 BC to help Tarentum against Rome.

literary_notes.text: Alcetas is defined by his ungovernable temper, which explains his exile and foreshadows his violent end.
'So madly raged' stresses the king's cruelty and prepares the people's night-time revolt.
Athens' ambition to reduce all Italy is undercut by its failure at Syracuse, which saved the Romans.
